materials.name: PMMA (Plexiglass)
materials.microgravity_behavior: Burns with a steady blue flame in quiescent microgravity. Flame spread is buoyancy-independent, producing a hemispherical flame front. Surface regression is uniform, and bubble formation in the melt layer is more pronounced without gravity-driven drainage.
materials.earth_vs_micro: Flame spread rate decreases 40-60% in microgravity. The flame is bluer and less luminous. In 1g, buoyancy-driven convection accelerates flame spread and produces a taller, more yellow flame.
materials.safety_recommendation: Avoid use in high-O2 environments. Use only in small quantities with fire barriers in exploration atmosphere (34% O2, 56.5 kPa). Consider replacement with fire-retardant polycarbonate where transparency is required.

materials.name: Cotton-Fiberglass Blend (SIBAL)
materials.microgravity_behavior: Exhibits steady flame spread with a flat flame front in microgravity. The fiberglass component acts as a structural backbone after cotton burns, leaving a fragile ash skeleton. Flame spread is uniform across sample width in low-flow conditions.
materials.earth_vs_micro: Flame spread rate decreases 30-50% in microgravity. In 1g, upward flame spread is significantly faster due to buoyant preheating of unburned material. Char pattern is more uniform in microgravity.
materials.safety_recommendation: Acceptable for standard ISS atmosphere with restrictions on total quantity. Requires re-evaluation for exploration atmosphere. Limit use near ignition sources and electrical equipment.

materials.name: Nomex
materials.microgravity_behavior: Shows borderline flammability in microgravity at standard atmosphere. Flames self-extinguish after brief propagation in most conditions. At elevated oxygen, sustained flame spread is possible but slow. Char formation is rapid and protective.
materials.earth_vs_micro: Marginally more flammable in microgravity at borderline conditions due to reduced heat loss. In 1g, flames rarely sustain on Nomex samples at standard atmosphere. The safety margin narrows in microgravity.
materials.safety_recommendation: Preferred material for fire-resistant applications in spacecraft. Acceptable for most ISS uses. Verify performance at exploration atmosphere conditions (34% O2). Combine with fire-retardant coatings for maximum safety.

materials.name: Teflon (PTFE)
materials.microgravity_behavior: Extremely difficult to ignite in microgravity. Does not sustain flame spread under any tested conditions at standard atmosphere. Even at 40% O2, only localized charring occurs without flame propagation.
materials.earth_vs_micro: Virtually non-flammable in both environments. No significant difference in flammability behavior between 1g and microgravity. Decomposition products are identical.
materials.safety_recommendation: Excellent fire safety choice. However, if heated above 400°C by an external fire, releases highly toxic fluorine compounds including hydrogen fluoride (HF) and carbonyl fluoride (COF2). Ensure adequate ventilation monitoring near potential heat sources.

materials.name: Polyethylene
materials.microgravity_behavior: Highly flammable in microgravity. Melting and dripping behavior changes dramatically — melt beads form on the surface rather than falling away, sustaining local burning. Flame spread is accelerated by melt accumulation in microgravity.
materials.earth_vs_micro: In 1g, melting and dripping can extinguish flames by removing hot fuel from the flame zone. In microgravity, melt stays in place, acting as a sustained fuel reservoir. This reversal makes polyethylene potentially more hazardous in microgravity.
materials.safety_recommendation: Minimize use aboard spacecraft. Replace with fire-retardant alternatives where possible. When polyethylene must be used, limit quantity and isolate from ignition sources with fire-resistant barriers.

materials.name: Silicone Rubber
materials.microgravity_behavior: Burns with a characteristic white-green flame and produces white silica ash. In microgravity, the ash remains on the surface forming an insulating layer that can self-extinguish the flame. However, cracking of the ash layer can lead to re-ignition.
materials.earth_vs_micro: In 1g, silicone rubber dripping and flowing can spread fire. In microgravity, the absence of dripping confines burning to the original surface but ash retention effects create unpredictable behavior. Flammability was higher than expected in SAFFIRE-II tests.
materials.safety_recommendation: Use with caution. The ash self-extinguishing effect is unreliable. Treat as moderately flammable for spacecraft design purposes. Prefer silicone formulations with added fire retardants.

materials.name: Kapton (Polyimide Film)
materials.microgravity_behavior: Extremely fire-resistant in microgravity. Does not sustain flame spread at standard atmosphere. Chars in place without melting. At elevated oxygen concentrations (>30%), slow surface burning may occur.
materials.earth_vs_micro: Consistently fire-resistant in both 1g and microgravity at standard atmosphere. One of the few materials showing nearly identical flammability behavior regardless of gravitational environment.
materials.safety_recommendation: Excellent choice for fire-critical applications. However, thermal decomposition releases toxic hydrogen cyanide (HCN) and carbon monoxide (CO). Ensure cabin atmosphere monitoring for these gases in areas where Kapton could be exposed to external heat sources.

materials.name: Velcro (Hook and Loop)
materials.microgravity_behavior: The hook-and-loop structure creates a high surface-area-to-volume ratio that enhances flammability. In microgravity, flame spreads through the material rapidly due to the open fibrous structure allowing oxygen access. Molten droplets remain attached rather than falling.
materials.earth_vs_micro: Flame spread rate is comparable in 1g and microgravity for the hook side due to the material's intrinsic structure dominating over buoyancy effects. The loop side shows reduced spread rate in microgravity.
materials.safety_recommendation: Minimize total surface area of Velcro exposed in spacecraft. Use fire-retardant Velcro alternatives (Nomex-based hook-and-loop) for critical applications. Avoid placing near electrical equipment or heat sources.

materials.name: Nylon
materials.microgravity_behavior: Melts and forms beads before igniting. In microgravity, melt beads adhere to the surface and can sustain flame. Produces dripping hazard in 1g but pooling hazard in microgravity. Flame is blue-yellow with moderate soot.
materials.earth_vs_micro: In 1g, nylon melts and drips, often self-extinguishing by removing molten fuel. In microgravity, melt pooling on the surface sustains combustion. This can result in higher effective flammability in microgravity.
materials.safety_recommendation: Use fire-retardant nylon grades for spacecraft applications. Limit use in areas near ignition sources. The melting behavior makes nylon more hazardous in microgravity than ground-based tests suggest.

materials.name: Kevlar
materials.microgravity_behavior: Extremely fire-resistant. Does not sustain flame in standard or moderately enriched oxygen atmospheres. Chars in place, maintaining structural integrity. Only burns at oxygen concentrations exceeding 29% in microgravity.
materials.earth_vs_micro: Consistently non-flammable in both environments under standard conditions. Fire performance is gravity-independent due to the inherent thermal stability of the aromatic polyamide structure.
materials.safety_recommendation: Excellent choice for structural fire barrier applications. Preferred for use in critical fire protection layers. Thermal decomposition above 500°C may release HCN — maintain atmospheric monitoring.

materials.name: Epoxy Composite
materials.microgravity_behavior: Burns on surface with delamination of composite layers. In microgravity, delaminated layers remain in place and can act as additional fuel. Produces thick black smoke with toxic volatiles. Flame spread occurs between composite plies.
materials.earth_vs_micro: In 1g, delaminated layers fall away, limiting fire propagation. In microgravity, the intact delaminated structure provides continuous fuel pathways. Smoke production is similar in both environments.
materials.safety_recommendation: Use fire-retardant epoxy formulations or phenolic resins for spacecraft structural applications. Consider brominated or phosphorus-based fire retardant additives. Ensure structural composites are covered with non-flammable surface layers.

materials.name: Cellulose (Paper)
materials.microgravity_behavior: Thin cellulose samples burn with a blue flame front that spreads steadily in microgravity. Ash retains original shape due to no gravity-driven fragmentation. Thicker samples may self-extinguish due to insufficient oxygen transport in quiescent microgravity.
materials.earth_vs_micro: Upward flame spread in 1g is 2-4x faster than in microgravity. Downward spread in 1g is comparable to microgravity horizontal spread. Char and ash behavior is significantly different — ash falls in 1g but remains in place in microgravity.
materials.safety_recommendation: Minimize loose paper and cellulose materials aboard spacecraft. Store in sealed fire-resistant containers. Replace with electronic documentation where possible. Cellulose wipes should be stored wet or in sealed bags.

materials.name: SIBAL Cloth
common_uses: Standard test material for NASA flammability testing
Reference material for flame spread studies
materials.microgravity_behavior: Primary reference material for SAFFIRE experiments. Burns with a uniform flame front in microgravity. Fiberglass structural grid maintains sample shape during and after combustion. Provides highly repeatable flame spread behavior making it ideal for benchmarking.
materials.earth_vs_micro: Flame spread rate is approximately 50% lower in microgravity at 20 cm/s airflow. The uniform burning behavior is maintained in both environments, making it an excellent comparative reference material.
materials.safety_recommendation: Used primarily as a test reference material. Actual spacecraft applications of similar cotton-fiberglass blends should follow cotton-fiberglass blend guidelines. Not commonly used as a functional material in spacecraft.

materials.name: Foam Insulation (Polyurethane)
materials.microgravity_behavior: Extremely flammable in microgravity. The cellular structure provides high surface area and trapped air pockets that promote rapid flame propagation. Burns with significant smoke and toxic gas generation including hydrogen cyanide (HCN) and isocyanates.
materials.earth_vs_micro: In 1g, molten foam drips and falls, sometimes spreading fire to surfaces below. In microgravity, foam melts and remains in place, acting as a continuous fuel source. Both environments show rapid flame spread through the cellular structure.
materials.safety_recommendation: Avoid polyurethane foam in spacecraft. Use fire-retardant alternatives such as melamine foam or silicone foam. If foam insulation is required, use only formulations meeting NASA-STD-6001 requirements and enclose in fire-resistant enclosures.

materials.name: Electrical Wire Insulation (Cross-linked ETFE)
materials.microgravity_behavior: Moderately fire-resistant. When ignited by electrical overload or arc, flame propagation along wire insulation is slow and often self-extinguishes in standard atmosphere microgravity. At elevated oxygen, sustained propagation occurs along wire bundles.
materials.earth_vs_micro: Wire insulation fire behavior is similar in both environments for horizontal orientations. Vertical upward propagation in 1g is faster due to buoyant preheating. In microgravity, wire bundle geometry becomes the dominant factor over gravity.
materials.safety_recommendation: Use cross-linked ETFE or equivalently rated insulation for all spacecraft wiring. Avoid wire bundle configurations that create chimney-like flow channels. Protect wire harnesses with fire-resistant wrapping in high-risk areas. Monitor wire temperatures for early fault detection.

materials.name: Polycarbonate
materials.microgravity_behavior: Burns with a yellow flame and produces moderate soot. Charring occurs rapidly, forming an insulating layer that can slow flame spread. In microgravity, char layer integrity is maintained better than in 1g, providing some self-protection.
materials.earth_vs_micro: Flame spread rate is approximately 30-40% lower in microgravity. The char layer is more effective at reducing flame spread in microgravity due to absence of buoyancy disrupting the char structure.
materials.safety_recommendation: Acceptable alternative to PMMA where transparency is required. Self-charring behavior provides partial fire protection. Use fire-retardant grades (V-0 rated) for spacecraft. Consider as a replacement for PMMA in high-O2 environments.
